summary: The book shifts from instructions to a public consecration ceremony as Moses washes and clothes Aaron and his sons, then anoints the sanctuary and Aaron before the assembled congregation. Moses presents a sin offering, a burnt offering, and a consecration ram, and later sprinkles blood and oil on Aaron, his sons, and their garments. The new priests must remain at the Tent of Meeting for seven days.
whyItMatters: This chapter puts the earlier offering rules into action and establishes the priests through a commanded, witnessed process that sets apart their bodies, clothing, workspace, and time.

context.author: The narrative reports Moses carrying out commands attributed to Yahweh; it does not identify the book's narrator or final compiler.
context.audience: The assembled congregation witnesses the consecration, while Aaron and his sons receive and obey its instructions.
context.date: The story is set during Israel's time at Sinai; the chapter itself does not date its composition.
context.setting: At the door of the Tent of Meeting, with the altar, sanctuary furnishings, priestly garments, offerings, and congregation present.
context.literaryForm: Consecration narrative structured by repeated reports that Moses acted as Yahweh commanded.

outline.heading: The congregation assembles
outline.note: Moses gathers Aaron, his sons, the ritual objects, and all the congregation at the Tent's entrance.

outline.heading: Washing, clothing, and anointing
outline.note: Aaron and his sons are dressed for office while the sanctuary, altar, and Aaron are anointed and sanctified.

outline.heading: The bull of the sin offering
outline.note: Aaron's family lays hands on the bull, and Moses uses its blood to purify and make atonement for the altar.

outline.heading: The ram of the burnt offering
outline.note: The entire prepared ram is burned as an offering made by fire.

outline.heading: The ram of consecration
outline.note: Blood marks each priest, selected portions are waved and burned, and oil and blood sanctify the priests and garments.

outline.heading: The seven-day consecration watch
outline.note: Aaron and his sons eat the assigned meal, burn leftovers, and remain at the entrance until their consecration is fulfilled.

keyVerses.text: Moses said to the congregation, “This is the thing which Yahweh has commanded to be done.”
keyVerses.why: This announcement frames the ceremony as a public act of obedience rather than Moses' private invention.

keyVerses.text: He poured some of the anointing oil on Aaron’s head, and anointed him, to sanctify him.
keyVerses.why: The verse names the ceremony's purpose for Aaron: he is anointed and set apart for priestly office.

keyVerses.text: He killed it; and Moses took some of its blood, and put it on the tip of Aaron’s right ear, and on the thumb of his right hand, and on the great toe of his right foot.
keyVerses.why: Aaron receives the consecration blood on ear, hand, and foot; the next verse repeats the same marks for his sons.

keyVerses.text: You shall stay at the door of the Tent of Meeting day and night seven days, and keep Yahweh’s command, that you don’t die: for so I am commanded.”
keyVerses.why: The final instruction shows that consecration includes a sustained seven-day obligation with a severe warning.

questions.question: Why is the whole congregation assembled for this ceremony?
questions.answer: Yahweh's command explicitly calls for the congregation to gather, and Moses tells them that what follows is commanded. The public setting makes Aaron's appointment and the actions that establish the priesthood visible to the community the priests will serve.

questions.question: What happens before any animal is offered?
questions.answer: Moses washes Aaron and his sons, clothes Aaron in the named garments, places the Urim and Thummim in the breastplate, and crowns him. He then anoints the sanctuary, altar, furnishings, basin, Aaron, and finally clothes Aaron's sons.

questions.question: What are the ephod, Urim, and Thummim?
questions.answer: The ephod is one of Aaron's priestly garments, secured by its own woven band. The Urim and Thummim are objects placed in the breastplate; this chapter names and locates them but does not explain their construction or use.

questions.question: What does anointing do in this ceremony?
questions.answer: Moses uses oil on the tabernacle, its contents, the altar and vessels, the basin, and Aaron. The repeated stated result is to sanctify them—that is, to set people and things apart for their designated sanctuary roles.

questions.question: Why does an altar need purification and atonement if it cannot sin?
questions.answer: Verse 15 says Moses applies blood to purify, sanctify, and make atonement for the altar. That use shows that atonement language in Leviticus can concern sacred-space preparation, not only the forgiveness of a morally guilty person.

questions.question: Who performs the sacrifices during the consecration?
questions.answer: Moses officiates throughout: he kills the animals, applies and sprinkles blood, burns altar portions, washes the burnt offering's parts, and directs the priests' meal. Aaron and his sons lay hands on the animals and receive the ritual actions during their installation.

questions.question: What does the blood on the right ear, thumb, and toe symbolize?
questions.answer: The rite marks Aaron and each son on the right ear, thumb, and big toe with blood from the consecration ram. The text does not assign a distinct meaning to any one body part, though the shared sequence clearly places all of them within the same priestly consecration.

questions.question: What happens to the consecration ram and bread?
questions.answer: Selected fat, the right thigh, and three breads are placed in the priests' hands, waved, and then burned; Moses receives the breast. The remaining meat and bread are boiled and eaten at the Tent's entrance, with leftovers burned.

questions.question: Why must Aaron and his sons remain for seven days under threat of death?
questions.answer: The text says the full period is required to complete their consecration and to keep Yahweh's command. It presents departure as a grave breach of the commanded process but does not give a further rationale for the duration or penalty here.

glossary.def: The commanded process of setting Aaron and his sons apart for priestly service.
A principal priestly garment placed on Aaron and secured with a skillfully woven band.
Objects placed in Aaron's breastplate; their purpose is not explained within this chapter.
Oil applied to sanctuary objects and Aaron to sanctify them for their assigned roles.

reviewer: Codex editorial agents; independent chapter review

before.text: The offering laws finish with a summary of rites commanded to Moses at Sinai and with the portions assigned to Aaron and his sons.

here.text: Moses assembles the people, washes and clothes Aaron’s family, anoints the sanctuary and Aaron, performs three offerings, and requires the new priests to remain at the Tent for seven days.

after.text: On the eighth day Aaron begins offering for himself and the people, blesses the congregation, and the promised divine glory appears with fire.
